newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe inflation seen off-target at 20 percent.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe inflation seen off-target at 20 percent.

text.p: Zimbabwe's annual inflation is likely to rise above 20 percent by mid-year, above the 17 percent target set by President Robert Mugabe's government, economic analysts said on Wednesday.

The state Central Statistical Office (CSO) said the southern African country's all-items consumer price index rose 5.4 percentage points in February from January and pushed the year-on-year inflation rate to 19 percent.

"It's unlikely to go down in the coming couple of months. There is a lot of inflationary pressure building up in the economy," said Edmore Tobaiwa, chief economist at Zimbabwe's National Chamber of Commerce (ZNCC).
"That pressure is likely to keep the (inflation) rate around or above 20 percent, even when one takes into account whatever efforts there will be to keep it down," he told Reuters.
The rise in February inflation was mainly due to a 12.6 percent rise in the price of food -- which is the largest component of the index -- and a four to nine percent hike in fuel prices.

Bread prices went up this week. There are also fears that electricity and telephone rates will follow, and that some local companies will also start increasing prices after the government raised import duty on finished products under a new tariff regime unveiled last month.

The central Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe says the expected price increases may stoke inflation, which the government battled to reduce from a peak of over 40 percent in 1992 to a seven-year low of 13.8 percent last November.

In a commentary, the bank said "efforts to reduce inflation could be frustrated by periodic adjustments to administered prices" but said the annual rate was unlikely to exceed 20 percent by June this year.

In its latest bulletin on the Zimbabwe economy and business trends, Standard Chartered Bank Zimbabwe said there were signs that inflation -- which has averaged 26.5 percent a year since 1990 -- would remain above 17 percent in 1997, leaving little scope for interest rate reductions or sustained exchange rate stability.

"The three main sources of inflation have been inter-related: the public sector deficit (which Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa now sees hitting 11 percent this year from an initial target of 8.5 percent), rapid money-supply growth of 28.5 percent annually since 1990, and Zimbabwe dollar depreciation," it said.

A local stock broker said on Tuesday Zimbabwean shares may trend lower in the coming week on the back of the higher February inflation figure, which might induce some funds to go liquid in anticipation of a rise in money market rates.

"The latest inflation figure may have an impact on the market. Some funds may decide to go liquid now in anticipation of rising interest rates and this may have a depressive impact on the market," said the broker, who declined to be named.
